## BSc Artificial Intelligence at Johannes Kepler University Linz

One university project involved satellite pattern classification. It gave me practical experience with the steps involved in improving and optimizing machine-learning models. I had trained neural networks before university, but formal study has helped me understand the process more systematically.

I enjoy both the theoretical and practical sides of the degree. Mathematics and computer science have long been among my strongest academic areas, and I am especially interested in turning mathematical ideas into working intelligent systems.

I entered the school through a competitive Grade 5 entrance examination. Roughly 1,000 students sat the examination that year. A major part of the project involved training a machine-learning model for plant-disease classification. This was one of the first times I saw how effectively a trained model could solve a physical-world problem, and it strongly influenced my decision to study AI more seriously.

I trained my first machine-learning model with a friend in 2023 using TensorFlow. My early work focused on classification and convolutional neural networks, including applications connected to the Smart Farm project.

Today, I spend a significant amount of time working with AI coding agents and using them to build full-stack systems. I think of myself primarily as an AI builder at this stage: someone who likes turning AI capabilities into working products and automation systems while continuing to strengthen the underlying machine-learning theory.

I am especially interested in agentic AI, AI agents, AI coding agents, machine learning, intelligent automation, AI research, and full-stack AI systems.

My earlier robotics work was largely about automating physical systems. AI made automation feel much more flexible and intelligent, and that connection still shapes the kinds of problems I want to work on.

Builder-first is probably the best description of how I learn: I usually understand a technology most deeply once I have tried to make something real with it. Formal university study is adding theory, mathematics, and research foundations to years of project-driven learning.

# How I work

## Ship the small version

I'd rather have a rough thing in someone's hands this week than a polished thing
next quarter. Every project I've finished started as a version I was slightly
embarrassed by. GauravGPT's first release was a single HTML file with a system
prompt in a `<script>` tag — that's the point. It shipped, people used it, and
the feedback told me what to build next far better than my own guesses would have.

## Make the complicated feel obvious

The interesting work in most software isn't the algorithm, it's the translation:
taking something genuinely complex and giving it a surface where the complexity
doesn't leak. A streaming chat response that appears instantly, an input that
grows as you type, a mobile keyboard that doesn't shove the layout off-screen —
none of that is glamorous, and all of it is the difference between a demo and a
product.

## Be honest about the edges

This applies to systems and to me. An AI that confidently makes something up is
worse than one that says "I don't know that." So this counterpart is built to
refuse: it only answers from what I've actually written down, it shows its
sources, and when it doesn't have something it hands you my email instead of
guessing. I hold my own claims to the same bar.

## Constraints are design tools

"No build step." "One file." "Must work offline." Picking a hard constraint early
kills a hundred bad architectural options for free and usually produces something
more durable than the unconstrained version would have been.

## Learn in public

Everything I build is on GitHub, including the parts that aren't finished. The
cost is that my mistakes are visible; the benefit is that I actually finish
things, and that people can see how I think rather than taking my word for it.

# Appogeny

Appogeny is a public web product I created for turning personal words, photos,
music, and small interactions into a single interactive page for someone. I
started building it in July 2026.

## The Experience

Instead of sending a long message or a conventional digital greeting card, a
creator shapes the message into chapters that the recipient moves through. The
creation flow starts with the occasion and feeling, builds a first draft from
selected chapters, lets the creator preview and personalise the result, and
then publishes it for sharing.

## Accounts, Sharing, and Privacy

Appogeny deliberately does not require user accounts. Publishing creates two
separate links:

- an unlisted recipient link that opens the finished page; and
- a private edit link that lets the creator change or delete it.

Recipient pages are unlisted rather than publicly listed or indexed. The
product centres on one interactive page for one person, not a public profile or
social feed.

## Status and Use

The product is live at [appogeny.app](https://appogeny.app). It has had roughly
20 users, including people beyond my immediate circle.

I started Appogeny as a personal product project and am open to developing it
into a larger commercial product or startup if there is enough genuine user
interest.

## What Building It Taught Me

Appogeny pushed me to think beyond whether the code works. I had to consider
product design, onboarding, privacy trade-offs, interaction design, sharing
flows, and whether someone who did not build the product could understand and
enjoy using it.

# Digital Counterpart

The engine behind **GauravGPT**, the thing you're talking to right now. A
conversational counterpart that represents me to recruiters and collaborators —
and, critically, one designed to keep unsupported claims from reaching the answer.

## The problem with the obvious version

The obvious version of this is a chatbot with your biography stuffed into a
system prompt. I built that (GauravGPT) and used it for a year. It has one fatal
flaw: asked about a job I never had, it will invent one, in my voice, confidently.
For a portfolio that's worse than useless — it's a liability.

## The fix: evidence records, support verification, and a refusal

My background lives in plain markdown and JSON in a `data/` directory. An ingest
step turns it into provenance-bearing evidence records and searchable chunks.
Every question runs through candidate retrieval, then a separate support check
against the original proposition. Retrieval scores select what to inspect; they
do not decide what is true.

The important part is what happens when support is missing. Each question clause
is marked supported, contradicted, insufficient, or not recorded. Only approved
claims reach the voice renderer; unsupported clauses become explicit uncertainty.

## Design decisions worth defending

- **Hybrid over pure vector.** On a corpus of a few hundred chunks, BM25 is not
  the weak sibling — it's frequently better, especially on proper nouns like
  school names and library names. Fusing the two beats either alone, and it means
  the app works with *zero* embedding keys configured.
- **Files over a CMS.** Updating my background is `git commit`, not a login.
  Human-editable markdown means I'll actually keep it current.
- **Claim citations in the UI.** Factual claims carry evidence IDs that resolve
  to a source, heading, excerpt, and locator.
- **Pluggable providers.** Vector, embedding, verifier, and renderer boundaries
  stay explicit. A lexical-only local index remains a supported fail-closed mode.

## Stack

Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), React 19.2, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4,
shadcn/ui, Framer Motion. Streaming via the Vercel AI SDK v7.

The model provider is pluggable behind one interface. An earlier prototype used
Gemma for its free-tier allowance; current deployment facts are read from runtime
configuration rather than maintained in this project narrative.

Retrieval is hand-rolled — BM25 plus cosine similarity — because on this corpus
size a vector database is infrastructure you maintain for no gain.

# GauravGPT

The original, 2024 version: a lightweight browser-based chatbot with a custom
persona, built as one HTML file with no build step, no bundler, and no backend.
The name now belongs to this site; that project is where it started.

## The idea

I wanted a conversational version of myself online, and I wanted it to be
genuinely simple to run. The constraint I set was: **one file, opens in a
browser, no install**. That ruled out every framework and forced the interesting
decisions to be about interaction rather than architecture.

## How it works

The whole app is `index.html` — markup, styles, and logic in one document. It
talks to [Puter.js](https://puter.com) for inference via `puter.ai.chat`, which
means no API key handling and no server of my own. Conversation history is kept
in a plain array in memory and replayed on each turn so the model has context.

## What I actually solved

- **Mobile keyboards.** Using `100dvh` instead of `100vh` so the virtual keyboard
  doesn't push the composer off-screen — a small fix that took an embarrassing
  amount of debugging and is the difference between usable and not on a phone.
- **Perceived speed.** Animated typing indicators and optimistic message
  rendering, so the interface responds the instant you hit send rather than
  after the model does.
- **Composer ergonomics.** Auto-resizing textarea capped at 120px with scroll
  fallback; `Enter` sends, `Shift+Enter` newlines.
- **Theming without a toggle.** Light and dark handled purely through
  `prefers-color-scheme` CSS variables — no JS, no flash of wrong theme.

## What I'd change

The persona lives in a hardcoded `SYSTEM_PROMPT` string, which means the model
will happily improvise biography it was never given. That single limitation is
the direct reason I built the Digital Counterpart: same idea, but grounded in
retrieval so it can only say things I've actually written down.

## Stack

Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3 custom properties, Puter.js. Deployed on
GitHub Pages.

# LinzSings

I developed LinzSings for the official AI Hackathon at Ars Electronica Festival
2026, held on September 11 and 12 at Grand Garage in Linz. The project won first
prize through the event's community vote.

## The Experience

LinzSings turns the history of Linz streets and public places into a listening
experience. A transmitter plays ambient music containing a hidden identifier
for a City of Linz street record. A visitor opens the app on another phone,
listens through the microphone, and sees the matching English-language story
after the signal has been decoded and verified.

The project uses the City of Linz open-data street catalogue, including current
and historical street names. It offers a way to discover the city through
sound instead of searching for a street name or scanning a code.

## How It Works

The live protocol encodes each record as a packet carried by four musical
frequencies. The browser finds the packet timing and preamble, decodes the
payload, checks its CRC, and matches the resulting Sonic ID against a local
public dataset before showing the place story.

Audio analysis runs entirely in the browser. The app does not record or upload
microphone audio, and the listening flow makes no API request after its data
bundle has loaded.

## Data and Stack

The repository includes a deterministic pipeline that normalizes 1,575 current
and historical records from the City of Linz street catalogue. It also includes
an optional source-grounded Mistral preprocessing path for editorial stories;
the live experience does not depend on an AI model.

The main stack is Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tone.js, the Web Audio API,
Zod, Vitest, and Playwright. The project is live at
[linz-cipher.vercel.app](https://linz-cipher.vercel.app), and the source is on
[GitHub](https://github.com/GauravAdz/linz-cipher).

persona, built as one HTML file with no build step, no bundler, and no backend.

I wanted a conversational version of myself online, and I wanted it to be
genuinely simple to run. The constraint I set was: **one file, opens in a
browser, no install**. That ruled out every framework and forced the interesting
decisions to be about interaction rather than architecture.

The whole app is `index.html` — markup, styles, and logic in one document. It
talks to [Puter.js](https://puter.com) for inference via `puter.ai.chat`, which
means no API key handling and no server of my own. Conversation history is kept
in a plain array in memory and replayed on each turn so the model has context.

- **Mobile keyboards.** Using `100dvh` instead of `100vh` so the virtual keyboard
  doesn't push the composer off-screen — a small fix that took an embarrassing
  amount of debugging and is the difference between usable and not on a phone.
- **Perceived speed.** Animated typing indicators and optimistic message
  rendering, so the interface responds the instant you hit send rather than
  after the model does.
- **Composer ergonomics.** Auto-resizing textarea capped at 120px with scroll
  fallback; `Enter` sends, `Shift+Enter` newlines.
- **Theming without a toggle.** Light and dark handled purely through
  `prefers-color-scheme` CSS variables — no JS, no flash of wrong theme.

The persona lives in a hardcoded `SYSTEM_PROMPT` string, which means the model
will happily improvise biography it was never given. That single limitation is
the direct reason I built the Digital Counterpart: same idea, but grounded in
retrieval so it can only say things I've actually written down.

I developed LinzSings for the official AI Hackathon at Ars Electronica Festival
2026, held on September 11 and 12 at Grand Garage in Linz. The project won first
prize through the event's community vote.

LinzSings turns the history of Linz streets and public places into a listening
experience. A transmitter plays ambient music containing a hidden identifier
for a City of Linz street record. A visitor opens the app on another phone,
listens through the microphone, and sees the matching English-language story
after the signal has been decoded and verified.

The project uses the City of Linz open-data street catalogue, including current
and historical street names. It offers a way to discover the city through
sound instead of searching for a street name or scanning a code.

The live protocol encodes each record as a packet carried by four musical
frequencies. The browser finds the packet timing and preamble, decodes the
payload, checks its CRC, and matches the resulting Sonic ID against a local
public dataset before showing the place story.

Audio analysis runs entirely in the browser. The app does not record or upload
microphone audio, and the listening flow makes no API request after its data
bundle has loaded.

The repository includes a deterministic pipeline that normalizes 1,575 current
and historical records from the City of Linz street catalogue. It also includes
an optional source-grounded Mistral preprocessing path for editorial stories;
the live experience does not depend on an AI model.

The main stack is Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tone.js, the Web Audio API,
Zod, Vitest, and Playwright. The project is live at
[linz-cipher.vercel.app](https://linz-cipher.vercel.app), and the source is on
[GitHub](https://github.com/GauravAdz/linz-cipher).

chunks.text:
An evidence-backed conversational portfolio designed to cite factual claims and abstain when support is insufficient.

Role: Solo build · Status: building · Year: 2026 · Tags: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Evidence verification, RAG, Tailwind CSS

chunks.title: Digital Counterpart
chunks.text:
The engine behind **GauravGPT**, the thing you're talking to right now. A
conversational counterpart that represents me to recruiters and collaborators —
and, critically, one designed to keep unsupported claims from reaching the answer.

chunks.title: Digital Counterpart
headings: The problem with the obvious version
chunks.text:
The obvious version of this is a chatbot with your biography stuffed into a
system prompt. I built that (GauravGPT) and used it for a year. It has one fatal
flaw: asked about a job I never had, it will invent one, in my voice, confidently.
For a portfolio that's worse than useless — it's a liability.

chunks.title: Digital Counterpart
headings: The fix: evidence records, support verification, and a refusal
chunks.text:
My background lives in plain markdown and JSON in a `data/` directory. An ingest
step turns it into provenance-bearing evidence records and searchable chunks.
Every question runs through candidate retrieval, then a separate support check
against the original proposition. Retrieval scores select what to inspect; they
do not decide what is true.

The important part is what happens when support is missing. Each question clause
is marked supported, contradicted, insufficient, or not recorded. Only approved
claims reach the voice renderer; unsupported clauses become explicit uncertainty.

chunks.title: Digital Counterpart
chunks.text:
- **Hybrid over pure vector.** On a corpus of a few hundred chunks, BM25 is not
  the weak sibling — it's frequently better, especially on proper nouns like
  school names and library names. Fusing the two beats either alone, and it means
  the app works with *zero* embedding keys configured.
- **Files over a CMS.** Updating my background is `git commit`, not a login.
  Human-editable markdown means I'll actually keep it current.
- **Claim citations in the UI.** Factual claims carry evidence IDs that resolve
  to a source, heading, excerpt, and locator.
- **Pluggable providers.** Vector, embedding, verifier, and renderer boundaries
  stay explicit. A lexical-only local index remains a supported fail-closed mode.

chunks.title: Digital Counterpart
chunks.text:
Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), React 19.2, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4,
shadcn/ui, Framer Motion. Streaming via the Vercel AI SDK v7.

The model provider is pluggable behind one interface. An earlier prototype used
Gemma for its free-tier allowance; current deployment facts are read from runtime
configuration rather than maintained in this project narrative.

Retrieval is hand-rolled — BM25 plus cosine similarity — because on this corpus
size a vector database is infrastructure you maintain for no gain.

chunks.title: GauravGPT
chunks.text:
The original, 2024 version: a lightweight browser-based chatbot with a custom
persona, built as one HTML file with no build step, no bundler, and no backend.
The name now belongs to this site; that project is where it started.

chunks.title: GauravGPT
chunks.text:
I wanted a conversational version of myself online, and I wanted it to be
genuinely simple to run. The constraint I set was: **one file, opens in a
browser, no install**. That ruled out every framework and forced the interesting
decisions to be about interaction rather than architecture.

chunks.title: GauravGPT
chunks.text:
The whole app is `index.html` — markup, styles, and logic in one document. It
talks to [Puter.js](https://puter.com) for inference via `puter.ai.chat`, which
means no API key handling and no server of my own. Conversation history is kept
in a plain array in memory and replayed on each turn so the model has context.

chunks.title: GauravGPT
chunks.text:
- **Mobile keyboards.** Using `100dvh` instead of `100vh` so the virtual keyboard
  doesn't push the composer off-screen — a small fix that took an embarrassing
  amount of debugging and is the difference between usable and not on a phone.
- **Perceived speed.** Animated typing indicators and optimistic message
  rendering, so the interface responds the instant you hit send rather than
  after the model does.
- **Composer ergonomics.** Auto-resizing textarea capped at 120px with scroll
  fallback; `Enter` sends, `Shift+Enter` newlines.
- **Theming without a toggle.** Light and dark handled purely through
  `prefers-color-scheme` CSS variables — no JS, no flash of wrong theme.

chunks.title: GauravGPT
chunks.text:
The persona lives in a hardcoded `SYSTEM_PROMPT` string, which means the model
will happily improvise biography it was never given. That single limitation is
the direct reason I built the Digital Counterpart: same idea, but grounded in

chunks.title: LinzSings

I developed LinzSings for the official AI Hackathon at Ars Electronica Festival
2026, held on September 11 and 12 at Grand Garage in Linz. The project won first
prize through the event's community vote.

chunks.title: LinzSings
chunks.text:
LinzSings turns the history of Linz streets and public places into a listening
experience. A transmitter plays ambient music containing a hidden identifier
for a City of Linz street record. A visitor opens the app on another phone,
listens through the microphone, and sees the matching English-language story
after the signal has been decoded and verified.

The project uses the City of Linz open-data street catalogue, including current
and historical street names. It offers a way to discover the city through
sound instead of searching for a street name or scanning a code.

chunks.title: LinzSings
chunks.text:
The live protocol encodes each record as a packet carried by four musical
frequencies. The browser finds the packet timing and preamble, decodes the
payload, checks its CRC, and matches the resulting Sonic ID against a local
public dataset before showing the place story.

Audio analysis runs entirely in the browser. The app does not record or upload
microphone audio, and the listening flow makes no API request after its data
bundle has loaded.

chunks.title: LinzSings
chunks.text:
The repository includes a deterministic pipeline that normalizes 1,575 current
and historical records from the City of Linz street catalogue. It also includes
an optional source-grounded Mistral preprocessing path for editorial stories;
the live experience does not depend on an AI model.

The main stack is Next.js 16, React 19, TypeScript, Tone.js, the Web Audio API,
Zod, Vitest, and Playwright. The project is live at
[linz-cipher.vercel.app](https://linz-cipher.vercel.app), and the source is on
[GitHub](https://github.com/GauravAdz/linz-cipher).

chunks.title: Smart Farm and Its Ecosystem
chunks.text:
Smart Farm and Its Ecosystem, also called the Autonomous Nursery, began at
Budhanilkantha School in 2023. It started with two people and later grew into a
larger robotics group.

The approximately 60 cm by 30 cm by 25 cm prototype combined embedded systems,
IoT, sensors, automation, and machine learning. Arduino and Raspberry Pi
controlled camera-based data collection, temperature, humidity, soil-moisture
and gas sensing, relays, water pumps, drip irrigation, filament-bulb heating,
fan-based cross-ventilation, and a cloud-connected monitoring and control
dashboard.

The sensors let the nursery sense its physical environment. Control software
closed the loop by adjusting irrigation, heating, and ventilation.
